COT on #forex: Dollar longs surge as euro selling accelerates

The rapid rebuilding of speculative dollar longs extended into the latest COT reporting week to 6 October, despite the greenback pausing its recent advance, with the broad Bloomberg Dollar Index ending the week little changed. This failed to deter dollar buyers, who lifted their aggregate net long against eight IMM currency futures by 40% to USD 35.4 billion, up sharply from just USD 6 billion three weeks earlier and moving back towards the multi-year peak of USD 50 billion reached in July.

Selling was led by the euro amid mounting political and fiscal concerns in Europe, particularly France, driving the speculative EUR net short to nearly 100k contracts, the largest since 2020 and equivalent to USD 14 billion. Dollar buying was otherwise broad-based, with speculators selling 41.7k MXN, 35.3k AUD, 12k NZD, 11.5k CAD and 6.5k GBP contracts. The yen was the main exception, attracting net buying of 6.9k contracts.

Much has already been written and said about President Trump's decision on Friday to ease sanctions on Russian diesel in an effort to bring down fuel costs ahead of the US midterm elections. I have made a point of keeping this feed focused on markets rather than politics, and intend to continue doing so.

However, the economic pressure behind the decision is clear, with diesel prices hovering near USD 200 per barrel and US consumers facing exceptionally high fuel costs. Russian supplies on the scale being discussed are unlikely to have more than a limited impact, especially compared to the potential political fallout from this decision. Indeed, New York ULSD futures fell just 3% on Friday to USD 4.74 per gallon, remaining within their recent 50-cent trading range. More importantly, additional Russian supplies would do little to address the underlying problem. The global distillate market remains exceptionally tight, primarily because of disrupted refinery operations and product exports from the Persian Gulf, compounded by reduced Russian refinery output.

The distinction matters: crude oil shipments from the Gulf have recovered significantly, but refined product flows remain severely constrained. With substantial refining capacity still offline, restoring crude supply alone will not resolve the diesel shortage. Moreover, redirecting Russian exports towards the US would do little to increase overall global availability. A sustained easing of distillate prices will ultimately require the restoration of refining capacity and product exports, particularly from the Middle East.

COT on #commodities: A broad rebound following two weeks of losses did little to change the selling bias among managed money accounts. According to the latest COT report, covering the week to 6 October, when the Bloomberg Commodity Index rose 1.2%, these traders remained net sellers across several key markets, including crude oil, natural gas, gold, copper, corn and cotton. Buying was concentrated in fewer contracts, led by sugar and soybeans. 

Energy: The combined WTI and Brent crude oil net long was cut for a third consecutive week, falling by 23k contracts to a two-month low of 313k, while the natural gas net short jumped to a two-and-a-half-year high.

Metals: The COMEX gold net long fell to a three-month low of 115k contracts, highlighting the contrast between short-term momentum traders and longer-term investors, whose continued ETF accumulation has lifted holdings to a four-year high. In copper, long liquidation accelerated despite a modest weekly price gain, with funds cutting their net long by 22% to a three-month low of 64.5k contracts.

Agriculture: Corn longs continued to be reduced following last month's record high, with a 60k-contract cut to a still elevated 317.4k occurring ahead of Friday's bearish WASDE surprise, which triggered the biggest one-day slump since 2023. Elsewhere, a 10.5% surge in sugar futures drove a 13% increase in the net long to 257.4k contracts, just below its 2023 record.

More in my Monday update.

#Grains: USDA supply shock sent corn futures tumbling on Friday.

US corn futures plunged by as much as the daily 30 cents trading limit on Friday, the most in three years, before settling down 20 cents, or 4.1%, at 480 cents per bushel, after the USDA's October WASDE report delivered a major bearish supply surprise. The department unexpectedly raised its 2026/27 US corn production forecast to 16.034 billion bushels, up from 15.800 billion in September and 1.9% above trade expectations. The increase was driven by a higher yield estimate of 181.2 bushels per acre, compared with 178.5 previously, pushing projected US ending stocks up by 282 million bushels to 1.849 billion, almost 10% above expectations. Global corn inventories were also revised higher to 280.44 million tonnes, adding to the bearish outlook.

The report dealt a significant blow to a recovery that began in mid-August, when concerns about damage from intense summer heat supported prices. Meanwhile, disruptions to Black Sea grain exports caused by the ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict had raised hopes of stronger demand for US supplies, offering some relief to farmers already struggling with elevated production costs.

Wheat followed corn lower after the USDA raised its US ending stocks forecast to 740 million bushels, above the 721 million expected. Soybeans, meanwhile, recovered from an initial slide to a six-week low to finish higher, despite upward revisions to US production and inventories. While the report reinforced expectations of ample grain supplies, the sharp selloff also leaves the market increasingly sensitive to any renewed export disruptions or signs of stronger-than-expected demand.

Friday's slump, led by corn, triggered a spike in trading volumes across the grains complex, likely accelerating long liquidation by managed money accounts. In the week to last Tuesday, these traders had already cut their net long corn exposure by 16% to 317k contracts, down from a record 431k reached last month.

Across the broader grain and soy complex, the combined net long position in six major futures contracts has fallen by 139k contracts over the past three COT reporting weeks to 6 October, retreating from a record high to 870k contracts. Despite the reduction, positioning remains historically elevated, at nearly eight times the five-year average of just 110k contracts, leaving the sector vulnerable to further long liquidation as seen on Friday.

(Bloomberg) -- Corn plunged by the most in three years after the US Department of Agriculture raised its outlook for yield and production of the top American crop, when most analysts expected a cut. 
The agency estimated corn output at about 16 billion bushels, up 1% from last month. Analysts surveyed by Bloomberg, on average, predicted production of 15.73 billion.
Futures dropped by their daily price limit of 30 cents, sliding 6% to $4.7025 a bushel, the lowest level since Aug. 11.

#Copper stocks monitored by the three major futures exchanges rose by 11.4 kt to just above 1 million tonnes this week, with the increase primarily driven by a Golden Week-related 20 kt build in Shanghai, lifting SHFE stocks to 58.7 kt. COMEX inventories also continued to climb, rising 4.8 kt to a fresh record high of 711.6 kt, meaning New York now accounts for around 71% of total monitored exchange stocks.
This concentration underlines how much of the recent global stock build remains tied to the US market, where metal has increasingly been drawn in and tied up. By contrast, LME stocks fell by 13.4 kt to 235.2 kt, highlighting that availability outside the US remains relatively tighter than the headline global total might suggest.

#Commodities: 

#Gold trades near USD 4,200, recovering from a challenging week that saw prices fall to a two-month low as bond yields surged to fresh multi-year highs. The rebound has been supported by a recovery in US Treasuries following a well-received 30-year bond auction, alongside some easing in oil prices, although fuel costs remain elevated. Gold ETF demand has remained remarkably resilient throughout the recent surge in yields, with total holdings rising to a fresh four-year high on Thursday. Combined with renewed Chinese demand following the Golden Week holiday, this underlying investment appetite is helping bullion recover and challenging recent attempts by short sellers to push prices lower.

Brent #crudeoil trades near USD 103, retreating from Thursday's high near USD 106 after Trump ruled out an attack on Iran ahead of the US midterm elections. This signals a potential three-week period of relative calm, which, provided Iran refrains from further escalation, could allow crude exports from the Gulf to remain elevated. However, the underlying stress in the oil market remains concentrated in refining capacity and the availability of refined products, particularly middle distillates such as diesel and jet fuel. Gulf product exports are estimated at around 50% of pre-war levels (Kpler), highlighting the continued supply shortfall. A sustained recovery in refinery operations and product exports will therefore be essential before the market can begin to normalise, even as crude flows continue to improve.

The Bloomberg Commodity Total Return Index is heading for its first weekly gain in three, up 1.6% at the start of Friday’s session, lifting its year-to-date advance to 35%. Despite persistent macroeconomic headwinds, all sectors are contributing to the recovery, once again led by energy, where natural gas and particularly diesel futures have posted strong gains. Perhaps surprisingly, given how the week has unfolded, precious metals occupy second place, with gold heading for its best weekly performance since early August. Industrial metals are also trading higher, albeit with more modest gains led by copper and zinc. Agriculture is contributing with most grain and soft commodity futures posting small weekly gains, led by soybeans, corn, sugar and cotton.
